name: Aptakube
tagline: A native desktop GUI for Kubernetes that lets you browse, edit and debug workloads across multiple clusters at once.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: Everything Aptakube does runs against your own kubeconfig, so there is no network, no data moat and nothing to phone home to. An agent can absolutely build you a local web dashboard that lists pods and deployments, tails logs, execs into containers and port-forwards, and it will feel great for the four resource types you actually look at. The gap shows up on resource breadth: Kubernetes has a hundred kinds plus whatever CRDs your operators dragged in, and covering them well is grinding work, not one-shot work. You also lose the native app: signed builds, auto-update, instant startup, multi-cluster tabs that stay responsive when a cluster is slow. This is a legitimate build if you are a one-cluster, ten-resource person, and a losing bet if you live in Kubernetes all day.
coreLoopDIY: A local browser dashboard that reads your kubeconfig, lists core workload resources per context with live watch updates, streams logs, opens a shell into a pod and port-forwards a service.
requirements: an existing kubeconfig with working cluster access
whatYouLose: Coverage of the long tail of resource kinds and CRDs, which is where the annoying debugging actually happens
A signed native app with fast cold start, auto-update and OS keychain integration
Multi-cluster tabs and side-by-side views that stay usable when one cluster is unreachable
Polished YAML editing with schema validation and diff-before-apply, instead of your hand-rolled textarea
Someone else keeping up with Kubernetes API deprecations every few months
moatNotes: The moat is not the API access, it is the thousand small interactions that make a cluster browser not feel like a homework project.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because a Kubernetes GUI is a tool you use under stress, at 2am, when something is on fire, and that is exactly when a half-finished dashboard that only knows about Deployments and forgot about StatefulSets becomes actively expensive. People pay a small one-time-ish license fee to skip that entire category of self-inflicted pain, and to get an app that opens in half a second instead of a dev server they have to remember to start. The DIY version is fun to build and genuinely fine for a hobby cluster. It is a bad trade if the cluster pays your salary.
notes: The honest version of this build is a personal log-tailer and pod browser, not a Lens replacement.
prompt:
Build a local-only Kubernetes dashboard I run on my own machine against my own kubeconfig. No accounts, no cloud, no telemetry.

Stack, no substitutions:
- Backend: Node 20 + TypeScript + Fastify, using @kubernetes/client-node.
- Frontend: React + Vite + TypeScript, plain CSS, xterm.js for terminals.
- Single repo, npm workspaces, one `npm run dev` that starts both.
- Server binds to 127.0.0.1 only. No auth layer, because it is localhost and it already has my cluster credentials.

Behaviour:
- Load kubeconfig from KUBECONFIG env var or ~/.kube/config. Expose all contexts, let me switch context from a dropdown in the header. Show the current context loudly and colour-code anything named like prod.
- Namespace selector, plus an "all namespaces" option.
- Resource views for exactly these kinds: Pods, Deployments, StatefulSets, DaemonSets, Services, Ingresses, ConfigMaps, Secrets, Jobs, CronJobs, Nodes, Events. Sortable tables, text filter, age column, status column.
- Use the watch API over a WebSocket so tables update live. Reconnect with backoff when a watch dies. Do not poll.
- Pod detail: containers, restart counts, resource requests/limits, recent events, and a log pane that streams live with follow, container picker, and a previous-container-logs toggle.
- Exec into a container with a real interactive shell via xterm.js.
- Port-forward a pod or service to a local port, with a list of active forwards and a stop button.
- View any object's YAML. Editing is allowed via a plain code editor that applies with a confirmation dialog showing the diff. Delete requires typing the object name.
- Secrets are masked by default with a per-field reveal button.

Explicitly out of scope: helm, CRD discovery, metrics or charts, RBAC-aware UI hiding, multi-user, packaging as a desktop app, tests beyond a couple of smoke tests on the kubeconfig parser.

Deliverables: working code, .env.example with KUBECONFIG and PORT, and a README that says how to run it and which kinds are supported. Fail loudly with a readable message if the cluster is unreachable.
